metaTitle: Where Do Bed Bugs Hide? Start With the Bed
metaDescription: Bed bugs hide in box springs, mattress seams, bed frames and headboards first, then sofas, walls and belongings. How to inspect a bedroom or hotel room.
h1: Where Do Bed Bugs Hide? Hiding Places From the Mattress Outward
dek: The spots bed bugs use, from the bed outward, with one published count of where they were found, how far the bugs travel to feed, and how to inspect a bedroom or hotel room.
excerpt: Bed bugs hide in box springs, mattress seams, headboards and bed frames first. Here is how far they roam, when they feed and how to inspect a bedroom or hotel room.

quickAnswer.lead: **Bed bugs hide closest to where people sleep: in the seams, piping and tags of the mattress and box spring, and in cracks of the bed frame and headboard.** That is [the EPA's list](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) for the area around the bed. In heavily infested rooms the agency says they also turn up in chairs and couches, drawer joints, electrical outlets and the junction of wall and ceiling.
bullets: The EPA's rule of thumb is that any crack that will hold a credit card could hide a bed bug.
Bed bugs readily travel 5 to 20 feet from established hiding places to feed, according to the EPA.

In a University of Kentucky count of bed bugs found in 13 infested apartments, 34.6 percent were in box springs, 22.6 percent in couches and chairs, 22.4 percent in mattresses and 13.4 percent in bed frames and headboards.
Adults are about 3/16 inch long, and Virginia Tech says the largest share of any bed bug population is always immature bugs, which are smaller still.
Bed bugs are active mainly at night, but a hungry bug may feed during the day, per the University of Kentucky.
Virginia Tech's guide says bed bugs feed every 5 to 7 days if a host is present and spend the other days digesting.

body.text: Where do bed bugs hide?

Bed bugs hide as close to the people they feed on as they can, so the first places to look are the piping, seams and tags of the mattress and box spring and the cracks in the bed frame and headboard. That is the list [the EPA's guide to finding bed bugs](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) gives for the area around the bed. The [University of Kentucky's bed bug fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef636) says the most common place to find them is beds or other areas where people rest or sleep, and that they prefer to hide close to where they feed.

The EPA adds that in heavily infested rooms they also turn up in the seams of chairs and couches, between cushions, in curtain folds, in drawer joints, in electrical outlets and appliances, under loose wallpaper and wall hangings, at ceiling-wall junctions and even in the head of a screw.

One data set shows where the bugs actually were. A University of Kentucky count of the bed bugs found in 13 infested apartments, reproduced as a chart in [an Indiana Department of Health brochure](https://www.in.gov/dA/b6df403476/IDOH-Bed-Bugs-Brochure_05-2025.pdf), put 34.6 percent in box springs, 22.6 percent in couches and chairs, 22.4 percent in mattresses and 13.4 percent in bed frames and headboards. The three parts of the bed together held about 70 percent, and apart from couches and chairs no other location in the chart held more than 3.1 percent. It is a small sample and the brochure does not describe how the count was made, so treat it as a rough guide.

The table below runs from the bed outward, which is the order an inspection follows; it is not ranked by those shares. For the wider picture of how infestations start, spread and end, see [the complete bed bug reference](/learn/bed-bugs).

body.text: Which parts of the bed do bed bugs hide in first?

None of the sources says which part of the bed is occupied first, but in the 13-apartment count the box spring held the most bugs: 34.6 percent, against 22.4 percent in mattresses and 13.4 percent in bed frames and headboards. Kentucky's fact sheet says bed bugs often hide in the seams, folds and crevices of the mattress, box spring, bed frame and headboard, and that they frequently hide within items stored under beds.
Mattress piping, seams and tags

Check every seam and fold around the mattress, plus the tag. Virginia Tech entomologist Dini Miller's guide, [How to Identify a Bed Bug Infestation](https://www.vdacs.virginia.gov/pdf/bb-identify1.pdf), names the mattress seams, the tufts and the area under the mattress tags as places where bed bugs gather in groups, and lists the seams and tag among the places fecal spots are more likely to be found when an infestation is small. The EPA adds rusty or reddish stains on sheets and mattresses, which come from bugs that were crushed. A separate guide shows [what bed bug signs on a mattress look like and what to do about them](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress).

body.text: The box spring

Look along the upper seams and underneath. Kentucky says box springs afford many places for bed bugs to hide, especially along the upper seams and underneath, where the bottom edge of the box rests on the frame, and that an underlying dust cover may have to be removed to get access for inspection. Virginia Tech lists fecal spots on the wood frame of the box spring, aggregations along wood creases in box springs and bed frames, and aggregations where the box spring fabric is stapled to the wood frame.
Bed frame and headboard

The frame and the headboard offer cracks, joints and screw holes. The EPA names cracks on the bed frame and headboard, and Virginia Tech adds the holes for set-in screws and the space behind the headboard, which it also lists as a place to find shed skins. Kentucky says the crevices of bed frames should be examined, especially if the frame is wood, and that a thorough inspection requires dismantling the bed and standing its components on edge.

body.needed: Photo of the back of a wooden headboard lit by a flashlight beam, showing a cluster of dark spots and a few bed bugs in a joint near a screw hole

body.text: Do bed bugs hide in nightstands, dressers and other furniture?

Yes, and upholstered seating matters more than bedside furniture. Kentucky calls upholstered chairs, recliners and sofas the next most likely areas after the bed and says to examine them carefully along the seams, skirts and folds of fabric. In the 13-apartment count, couches and chairs held 22.6 percent of the bugs, about the same share as mattresses, while nightstands held 0.2 percent. The EPA lists the seams of chairs and couches, the spaces between cushions and drawer joints among the places bugs turn up in a heavily infested room.

Bedside furniture is still on the inspection list. Kentucky says nightstands and dressers may need to be emptied, examined inside and out, and tipped over so the woodwork underneath can be inspected. If a bug you find on furniture does not look right, [a comparison of the insects most often mistaken for bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs) covers carpet beetles, bat bugs and other look-alikes.
Can bed bugs hide in walls, baseboards and outlets?

Yes, though these spots held a small share of the bugs in the 13-apartment count: 2.3 percent for walls and ceilings and 1.4 percent for baseboard areas. Kentucky says bed bugs initially tend to be concentrated around beds, sofas and other sleeping and resting areas, and may disperse elsewhere if an infestation is allowed to persist.

Kentucky's list of other common hiding places includes the edge of wall-to-wall carpeting, especially behind beds and sofas, cracks in wood molding, ceiling-wall junctions, and the spaces behind wall-mounted pictures, mirrors, outlets and switch plates. The EPA adds electrical outlets and appliances, loose wallpaper, wall hangings and screw heads. Virginia Tech's list of aggregation sites includes behind loose wallpaper, behind chipped paint, behind baseboards, inside baseboard heaters and under the base of an air conditioner.

Wall and ceiling clusters are easy to misread. Dini Miller's guide includes a photograph of an apartment ceiling that first looked like mold or mildew from a moisture problem upstairs; on closer inspection it was many bed bug aggregations, and the black material was fecal spotting. If a dark patch on a ceiling or wall edge looks like mold, check it closely for bugs, skins and tiny eggs before deciding what it is.
Walls and ceilings also serve as routes. According to Kentucky, bed bugs can crawl from room to room, or from floor to floor, through cracks and openings in walls, floors and ceilings.
How far do bed bugs travel from their hiding places?

The EPA says bed bugs will readily travel 5 to 20 feet from established hiding places to feed. The sources used here give no maximum distance. Kentucky says bed bugs crawl rapidly over floors, walls, ceilings and other surfaces but do not fly or jump, and that they will crawl longer distances in search of a meal when they have to, even though they prefer to hide close to where they feed.
By that measure, a baseboard or outlet across a room can still be within range of the bed, which is why an inspection does not stop at the mattress.
When do bed bugs come out of hiding?

Mostly at night. Kentucky says bed bugs are active mainly at night and usually bite people while they are sleeping, though a hungry bug may also feed during the day, especially if that is when the occupant normally sleeps. The EPA agrees: they are primarily active at night, but a hungry bug will seek a host in full daylight. A meal does not take long. The EPA gives 3 to 12 minutes, and Kentucky says engorgement takes about 3 to 10 minutes.

Between meals the bugs are out of sight. Virginia Tech's guide says bed bugs feed every 5 to 7 days if a host is present and spend the days in between digesting. They excrete part of each meal as semi-liquid waste, deposited wherever they go after feeding, which dries into the black spots described below.

Size is the other reason they go unseen. Virginia Tech says an unfed adult is about 3/16 inch long and can look like a flat disc, and that the largest share of any bed bug population is always immature. Immature bugs are smaller than adults and translucent whitish-yellow, and the youngest nymphs are hard to see unless they are moving or have just fed; Kentucky describes newly emerged nymphs as no bigger than a pinhead. [How to recognize each life stage](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like) is covered in its own guide, and [what the small black specks really are](/blog/black-bed-bugs) in another.
How small a gap can a bed bug squeeze into?

A crack that will hold a credit card is enough. The EPA says bed bugs are only about the width of a credit card, so if a crack will hold one, it could hide a bed bug. Kentucky's yardstick is a toothpick: it says their flattened bodies let them fit into tiny crevices no wider than one. That is why the lists above are full of seams, joints, screw heads and the gaps behind trim rather than flat surfaces.

Eggs are tinier still. The EPA describes eggs and eggshells as tiny, about 1/25 inch (1 millimeter), and Virginia Tech compares an egg to the head of a pin and says eggs are pearl-white with obvious eyespots once they are more than 5 days old. Kentucky says eggs hatch in about a week at room temperature.
Do bed bugs hide in luggage, clothing and belongings?

Yes, and that is how they get into a home. Kentucky says bed bugs are easily transported into dwellings on luggage, clothing, beds, furniture and belongings. The EPA's page on [protecting your home from bed bugs](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/protecting-your-home-bed-bugs) calls them great hitchhikers that move from an infested site to a new home on furniture, bedding, luggage, boxes and clothing. Virginia Tech's guide says bed bugs have to be brought into a home, for example in luggage after a trip or on a piece of used furniture.

Once inside, belongings become hiding places. Virginia Tech lists books, stuffed animals and picture frames, plus the framing under a closet bar and the interior frame of closet doors. Kentucky adds clothing and clutter in closets and book bindings, and also names the insides of clocks, phones, televisions and smoke detectors.

body.title: Bites are a poor way to find the hiding place
body.text: Virginia Tech says bite reactions vary so much from person to person that bites are not a good way to diagnose an infestation, and the EPA calls bites a poor indicator. Kentucky cites studies in infested apartments suggesting about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly.
How do you inspect a bedroom for bed bugs?

Start with the bed and work outward, looking for evidence as well as live bugs. Bites alone cannot confirm anything ([what bed bug bites look like and how to tell for sure](/blog/bed-bug-bites) explains why), so look for the physical signs. Kentucky says the things to look for are the bugs themselves, the shed skins of the nymphs and the blackish fecal spots. The EPA's list of signs covers rusty or reddish stains on sheets and mattresses, dark spots of excrement about the size of a printed dot that may bleed into fabric the way a marker would, eggs and eggshells, shed skins, and the live bugs themselves.

body.text: Dini Miller's guide gives a way to tell bed bug spots from German cockroach droppings: first look for shed skins or hatched eggs nearby, and if there are none, touch the spots. Bed bug spots feel smooth because they are dried blood, while German cockroach droppings tend to feel granular. A longer guide covers [what bed bug droppings and stains look like, and the marks they get confused with](/blog/bed-bug-stains-poop-droppings-canada).

items: Strip the bed and look over the sheets and mattress cover for rusty stains, dark spots and bugs in the folds.
Work all the way around the mattress, checking the piping, seams, tufts and tag.
Lift the mattress off and inspect the box spring: the upper seams, the underside where the bottom edge rests on the frame, creases in the wood and the staples that hold the fabric to the frame.
Take the frame apart if you can, stand the pieces on edge, and check the joints, cracks and screw holes, then look behind the headboard.
Check upholstered chairs, recliners and sofas along the seams, skirts, fabric folds and the gaps between cushions.
Empty the nightstand and dresser drawers, check the joints and the woodwork underneath, and pull out anything stored under the bed.

Follow the room's edges: baseboards, carpet edges, ceiling-wall junctions, the areas around outlets and switch plates, the backs of pictures and mirrors, and the curtain folds and pleats near the rod.
Finish with the closet door frames and the belongings stored nearby.

body.text: Tools that help

items: **Flashlight.** Kentucky calls a flashlight useful for dimly lit areas.

**Interceptor cups.** Kentucky describes small plastic dishes that wandering bed bugs crawl or fall into and cannot escape, typically placed under the legs of beds and seating, and a separate guide covers [how to read an interceptor trap](/blog/bed-bug-interceptor-traps-canada).
**A credit card as a gauge.** The EPA uses it to show which gaps are large enough to hide a bug.
**Trained dogs.** Kentucky notes that some companies use specially trained dogs to help find small, dispersed infestations, and that reliability may vary from one canine inspection to the next.

body.text: How do you check a hotel room for bed bugs?

Check the bed first, starting at the pillow end. The University of Kentucky's advice for travelers is to take a moment to inspect beds, with a flashlight for dimly lit areas, and most of the points below come from that advice.

items: **Sheets and mattress.** Kentucky says to examine the bed sheets and the seams of the mattress, and perhaps the box spring, especially along the head (pillow end) of the bed.

**Headboard.** Kentucky says some experts check behind headboards because they are a frequent hiding place in hotel rooms, but it warns that headboards are heavy and cumbersome and that untrained people should not try to remove one. Look at the edges, joints and whatever gap you can see.

**Luggage rack.** A photo caption on the EPA's home-protection page, linked above, says to inspect the luggage rack in a hotel room, and Kentucky suggests keeping luggage up off the floor on a stand, table or other hard surface instead of stowing it on the floor or another bed.
**Nightstand and nearby edges.** The general hiding-place lists above also name drawer joints, outlets and curtain pleats, though none of the sources gives a hotel-specific order for them.
**If you find bugs.** Kentucky says guests can request another room, preferably in a different area of the hotel, because infestations sometimes extend to nearby units.
**When you get home.** If you had itchy welts suggestive of bites during the stay, Kentucky's advice is to put all clothing directly into the washer and dryer on returning home.

body.text: Finding nothing is not proof of nothing. Virginia Tech says that in a new infestation, a hotel room for example, bed bug evidence may be very hard to find, but because the largest share of a population is immature there is always a chance of finding cast skins. It also notes that a person bitten while traveling may not react for several days, and that bites noticed after getting home do not mean the home is infested.
What should you do after finding bed bug hiding places?

Confirm what you found before treating anything. If the bug or the specks might be something else, [the guide to bugs that get mistaken for bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs) helps you rule things out, and if what you found is an empty shell, [a guide to bed bug shells, casings and shed skins](/blog/bed-bug-shells-casings-shed-skins-canada) covers whether it still means an active problem. Once the bugs are confirmed, [the step-by-step plan to get rid of bed bugs](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs) explains what to do with the bed, the room and your belongings.

faqs.question: Can bed bugs live inside a mattress?
faqs.answer: The sources point to the outside of the mattress and to the box spring under it. The EPA lists the piping, seams and tags of the mattress and box spring, the University of Kentucky says bed bugs often hide in the seams, folds and crevices of the mattress, and Virginia Tech's guide names the seams, tufts and the area under the tags as places they gather in groups. In a University of Kentucky count from 13 infested apartments, box springs held 34.6 percent of the bugs and mattresses 22.4 percent.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs come out during the day?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, though mainly they feed at night. The University of Kentucky says bed bugs are active mainly at night and usually bite people while they sleep, but a hungry bug may also feed during the day. The EPA says a hungry bed bug will seek a host in full daylight. Virginia Tech says bed bugs feed every 5 to 7 days if a host is present and spend the days between meals digesting.

faqs.question: Can bed bugs hide in walls?
faqs.answer: They use the cracks and fixtures in and around walls. The EPA lists electrical outlets, loose wallpaper, wall hangings, ceiling-wall junctions and screw heads. The University of Kentucky says they can crawl from room to room or floor to floor through cracks and openings in walls, floors and ceilings. Virginia Tech also lists baseboard heaters, chipped paint and the area behind baseboards. In one University of Kentucky count from 13 infested apartments, walls and ceilings held 2.3 percent of the bugs found.

faqs.question: How small a space can bed bugs fit into?
faqs.answer: Any gap that will hold a credit card, according to the EPA, which says bed bugs are only about the width of a card. The University of Kentucky says their flattened bodies let them fit into tiny crevices no wider than a toothpick. An unfed adult is about 3/16 inch long and can look like a flat disc, per Virginia Tech, which is why seams, joints, screw holes and the space behind trim all count as hiding places.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs hide in clothes and luggage?
faqs.answer: Yes. The University of Kentucky says bed bugs are easily transported into dwellings on luggage, clothing, beds, furniture and belongings, and Virginia Tech's guide describes bed bugs arriving in luggage after a trip or on used furniture. Inside a home, Kentucky also names clothing and clutter in closets, and Virginia Tech lists books, stuffed animals and picture frames.

faqs.question: Can you have bed bugs without any bite marks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Virginia Tech says bite reactions vary so much that a person may not react at all, which can let an infestation go unnoticed until the population grows enough for the bugs to be seen. The University of Kentucky cites studies in infested apartments suggesting about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly. Virginia Tech calls bites an unreliable indicator and says to learn the other signs: fecal spots, shed skins and clusters of bugs.
